                          MOTION TO DISMISS AND ANSWER OF

       In accordance with Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal

Energy Regulatory Commission,1 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM) submits this Motion to

Dismiss and Answer in response to the Complaint filed by the Pennsylvania Public Utility

Commission (PA PUC) on August 17, 2026. The Complaint challenges PJM’s methodology for

selecting “market efficiency projects” 2 under Schedule 6, Section 1.5.7 of PJM’s Operating

Agreement, which governs the Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (RTEP) process. PA PUC

proposes certain alternative amendments to the Operating Agreement that are designed to “include

the impact of all (benefitting and non-benefitting) zones when calculating consumer benefits for

the purposes of market efficiency projects” and asks that the Commission direct PJM to implement

PA PUC’s proposed amendments. 3

       The Complaint proposes a major paradigm shift in how PJM analyzes market efficiency

projects, one that PJM stakeholders have previously rejected. The Complaint also rests on a

profound misunderstanding: that participating in an RTO somehow guarantees consumers in a

        In each case, the Commission-accepted Benefit/Cost Ratio exceeds PJM’s requisite 1.25:1

ratio, often by one or more orders of magnitude (e.g., Projects 218, 651, 704, and 756). And, in

each case, the benefits of the market efficiency project exceeded the cost. Even the two projects

PA PUC cites in its testimony as supportive examples for its preferred methodology—Project 9A

and Project 644+908—posted substantial benefits when considering only the beneficiaries and

when considering all of the zones. Project 9A of 2016 has a Benefit/Cost Ratio of 2.48, and Project

644+908 has a Benefit/Cost Ratio of 1.99. Other projects, like Project 733 and Project 525 have

equivalent benefits whether considering only the beneficiaries or only the zonal benefits because

every zone benefitted from those projects. Thus, while Mr. Ming suggests that the Benefits/Cost

Ratios for those projects were inflated due to PJM’s analysis, 4 the results speak for themselves.

Mr. Ming’s testimony also suffers from a number of fundamental errors, including mathematic

and modeling errors, which are detailed below in section III.B and in Mr. Horger’s Testimony.

       Moreover, PA PUC’s proposed replacement rate—treating the increase in Load Energy

Payment and Load Capacity Payment as a negative benefit—is inferior to the status quo and would

ensure that congestion inefficiencies continue and that beneficiaries of artificially low congestion

prices extract an unjust and unduly discriminatory benefit at the expense of other zones.

I.     MOTION TO DISMISS

       The Commission should dismiss the Complaint because it suffers from several critical

defects. First, the Complaint is purely speculative and not based on any current or imminent

injuries that the Commission could redress. Every internal market efficiency project of the last

decade has benefitted consumers in the PJM-wide region. PA PUC fails to demonstrate that PJM’s

existing project or even projects that are likely to be developed. The Complaint only outlines what

PA PUC considers improvements to the Tariff, not changes designed to address existing harm.

Moreover, as demonstrated in Table 1 of Mr. Horger’s Testimony and further described in the

Answer below, PA PUC’s complaint is not based on any actual injury. Every internal market

efficiency project of the last decade has benefitted PJM’s consumers.

       Second, the Complaint fails to satisfy requirements of Rule 206 governing the contents of

a complaint because it does not “[c]learly identify the action or inaction which is alleged to violate

applicable statutory standards or regulatory requirements” 5 or explain how those standards have

been violated. 6 PA PUC conspicuously left those requirements unexplained in Section VII of its

Complaint. 7 That is because the Complaint does not identify any instance of PJM violating its

Tariff, the Federal Power Act (FPA), or any Commission regulation.

II.    BACKGROUND

       Transmission congestion results from constraints in the transmission system and occurs

when available, least-cost energy cannot be delivered to all load because existing transmission

facilities are inadequate to deliver that energy to one or more areas. The consequence of

transmission congestion is that lower-cost generation cannot serve the load, requiring PJM to

dispatch higher-cost generation in the transmission-constrained area to meet the load. Therefore,

wholesale customers in transmission-constrained areas experience higher relative costs for power

determine projections of future congestion based on anticipated transmission upgrades.

       A. The Commission Grants PJM Full RTO Status and Approves PJM’s Approach

        B. Congestion in Pennsylvania and on the Delmarva Peninsula Reinforced the Need

The Delmarva Peninsula, in particular, was especially vulnerable to congestion due to its

insufficient local generation and a shortage of high-voltage transmission lines. In the years leading

2001, and 860 in the first eight months of 2002, with costs of $20 million, $59 million, and $16

        C. Orders Accepting Market Efficiency Provisions

       In 2006, PJM proposed a series of tariff amendments that would allow it to select “market

efficiency projects”—transmission enhancements or expansions developed to relieve economic

constraints.      Specifically, PJM proposed to preserve its traditional focus on unhedgeable

congestion but with additional emphasis on other congestion metrics, including:            (1) total

production costs; (2) total load payments; (3) total generator revenue; (4) zonal load payments;

(5) zonal [FTR] credits; (6) total transmission system losses; and (7) total capacity payments. 29

       Based on those metrics, PJM would then analyze whether reliability-based projects already

in the RTEP would provide sufficient additional benefits to justify expanding, modifying or

accelerating a particular transmission project. 30 PJM would also determine whether new projects

would provide sufficient benefits to justify adding them to the plan. In addition, PJM would

evaluate the extent to which demand response or new generation could eliminate the need for an

economic-based upgrade. The Commission conditionally accepted PJM’s filing but required PJM

to make a compliance filing explaining more fully how it would “weigh, consider and/or combine

the metrics in determining the net social economic benefits of a project.” 31 Finding PJM’s

compliance filing lacking detail, the Commission again ordered PJM to file another compliance

filing with a “formulaic approach to choosing economic projects proposed to reduce congestion”

and describing how any metrics would be calculated. 32

In other words, the congestion represents inefficiency on the system because the customers on both

sides of the constraint are not paying equitable costs.

III.   ANSWER

       A. PA PUC Has Not Met the Burden of Showing PJM’s Market Efficiency
          Framework is Unjust, Unreasonable, or Unduly Discriminatory or Preferential

       If the Commission declines to dismiss the Complaint, the Commission should reject PA

PUC’s arguments because they fail to demonstrate that PJM’s current market efficiency process is

unjust and reasonable. Instead, the Complaint only demonstrates that PA PUC fundamentally

misunderstands important components of that process.



                                                 14
        PA PUC makes a number of unsupported and baseless assertions, claiming that PJM

“discriminat[es] against a subset of loads,” “exclude[s] a subset of customers from their

‘consumer’ benefits metric,” and “act[s] in the interests of a subset of consumers … at the expense

of other consumers” when it selects market efficiency projects. 47           These claims rest on

fundamentally flawed assumptions about RTO operations. Most prevalent among PA PUC’s false

assumptions is that load located on the low side of a transmission constraint has an ongoing

entitlement to maintain the lower costs from which it benefits merely because it has restricted

access to lower-cost generation compared to its neighbors. 48 No such entitlement exists. The

purpose of PJM’s market is to ensure an efficient market and to optimize efficient pricing for all

users, not to maintain a price preference for certain zones that benefit from transmission

congestion. 49

        As noted by Mr. Horger, congestion represents inefficiency on the system because the

customers on both sides of the constraint are not paying equitable costs. The “non-constrained”

areas are benefiting from this inefficiency from lower LMPs while the “constrained” areas are

being harmed with higher LMPs. 50 Removal of the congestion removes the inefficiency on the

system resulting in equitable costs to all customers. Importantly, the customers in the “non-

constrained” areas who are benefiting from the inefficiency will not have to pay the costs from the

upgrade that removes the inefficiency. Only customers on the “constrained” areas will need to

pay for the removal of the congestion inefficiency.

       PJM’s market efficiency program is firmly based on the Commission’s guidance in Order

No. 2000 that RTOs should “ensure that the generators that are dispatched in the presence of

transmission constraints must be those that can serve system loads at least cost, and limited

transmission capacity should be used by market participants that value that use most highly.”51

       B. Mr. Ming’s Testimony is Critically Flawed

11   present value of the benefits and costs (e.g., discount rate and annual revenue requirement)

12   are among the assumptions that are considered by the PJM Board each year to be used in

13   the economic planning process. The Benefit/Cost Ratio is expressed as follows:

14           Benefit/Cost Ratio = [Present value of the Total Annual
15           Enhancement Benefit for the 15 year period starting with the RTEP
16           Year (defined as current year plus five) minus benefits for years
17           when the project is not yet in-service] ÷ [Present value of the Total
18           Enhancement Cost for the same 15 year period]

10   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE CONGESTION AS USED IN THIS CONTEXT.

11   A.   As described above, market efficiency congestion (i.e., transmission congestion) occurs

12        when the least costly resources that are available to serve load in a given region cannot be

13        dispatched because the physical limits of certain transmission facilities constrain power

14        flow on the system. This is particularly true in PJM where power often flows from lower-

15        priced generating resources in western zones to load centers in the East. The lowest-priced

16        energy is often constrained from flowing freely to those load centers. When this occurs,

17        PJM’s system operator must dispatch higher-cost resources to serve load. This results in

18        LMP differences and congestion on the system. The congestion generally increases system

19        production costs and LMPs. It also results in increased wholesale customer payments for

20        electric energy.

22        year planning horizon in order to identify the potential economic benefit of proposed

23        transmission projects. PJM conducts market simulations that show the extent to which
